title: How do hospitals and health systems work, and what matters in a healthcare case?
description: Healthcare economics for case interviews: capacity, beds, length of stay, patient flow, payers and public goals, with a worked bed-capacity example.
hook: Healthcare cases often involve public systems where the goal is not profit but better care within a budget. They reward clear thinking about capacity and flow, and sensitivity to patients and staff.
body:
Who pays and what success means

Depending on the country, care is paid for by governments, insurers or patients. In public systems, success means better outcomes, shorter waits and staying within budget. Do not force a profit lens onto a public goal (see public sector cases).

The measures that matter

  • Bed occupancy and length of stay.
  • Waiting times at each stage.
  • Readmission rates, a sign of quality.
  • Staffing levels and costs.

A worked example: why length of stay matters

A ward has 30 beds. If the average stay is 6 days, it can treat about 30 × 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 1,825 patients a year. Cut the average stay to 5 days through earlier discharge, and capacity rises to about 2,190, roughly 20% more patients with the same beds.

Typical healthcare case questions

  • Why have emergency waiting times doubled? (worked here)
  • How can a hospital cut costs without harming care?
  • Should a health system invest in community clinics?
  • Why is a new drug selling below forecast? (see pharma)

Capacity is not just the number of beds

A 30-bed ward operating at 85% average occupancy has 30 × 365 × 85% = 9,308 occupied bed-days per year, approximately. With an average length of stay of six days, it can complete about 1,551 stays annually. At five days per stay, theoretical completed stays rise to roughly 1,862, a gain of about 20% if patient demand, staffing, admissions and care quality allow it. This is a hypothetical operational calculation, not a clinical target.

Why include occupancy? A ward cannot reliably run at 100% occupancy every day and still absorb unpredictable arrivals, discharge delays and changes in patient acuity. Shortening stay is also not automatically good: premature discharge can increase readmissions or worsen outcomes. A rigorous recommendation tests both throughput and quality.

For emergency-department waiting times, draw the patient journey: arrival, triage, diagnostics, treatment, decision, and discharge or admission. Ask at which step the queue has grown. More nurses at triage may not fix a queue caused by no inpatient beds for admitted patients. Compare arrivals per hour with effective service capacity, paying special attention to peak periods and case mix.

In a public hospital case, the objective may be access and outcomes within a budget, not profit maximisation. Make that explicit. Finish with a pilot measure: median and high-percentile wait time, readmissions, staff workload and clinical safety, alongside cost per treated patient.
